title: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY BEFORE ANYONE TOUCHED ANYONE: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT PORNOGRAPHY THAT THE CHURCH CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE
paragraphs: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY BEFORE ANYONE TOUCHED ANYONE: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT PORNOGRAPHY THAT THE CHURCH CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE

You may have never cheated physically. You may have never touched another person. But what if the secret you keep deleting from your phone is revealing something about your heart that Jesus has been trying to heal for years? This is not just about pornography. It is about the battle for your soul, the people your choices affect, and the Savior who refuses to leave you chained to what He died to free you from.
There is a kind of silence that happens after the screen goes dark.
Nobody sees it.
Nobody hears it.

The room is exactly as it was a few minutes earlier. The door is still locked. Your phone is still in your hand. Your spouse may be sleeping beside you. Your children may be in another room. Your Bible may be sitting on the nightstand.
But something inside you feels different.
Again.
You promised God you would stop.
Again.
You told yourself this would be the last time.
Again.
And now you are staring at the ceiling, wondering how someone who genuinely loves Jesus can keep returning to something that leaves them feeling so far from Him.
Maybe you whisper a prayer.
Maybe you cannot even find the words.
Maybe you have become so familiar with the cycle that you no longer cry.
And perhaps the most frightening part is not that you have fallen again.
Perhaps it is that you are beginning to wonder whether you should even feel convicted anymore.
Jesus did not expose the darkness of the human heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposed it because He came to save them.
And what He said about adultery may confront you more deeply than you expect.
Because according to Jesus, adultery is not merely a question of what your body has done.
It is also a question of what your heart has deliberately embraced.
And that changes everything.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus says:

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Those words are from the King James Version.
Read them slowly.
Jesus does not say that every experience of sexual attraction is adultery.
He does not say that accidentally noticing someone attractive makes you guilty of sexual unfaithfulness.
He does not say that temptation itself is identical to surrendering to temptation.
He identifies something much more intentional.
Looking in order to lust.
The Greek text makes this distinction especially important.
Matthew 5:28 contains the expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
In this context, the phrase describes looking at a woman with the purpose or orientation of desiring her lustfully.

The verb epithymeō can refer to desire in different contexts. Desire is not automatically sinful simply because it is desire. But here, Jesus is addressing covetous sexual desire directed toward someone.
And the phrase that follows is devastating:
ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ
Ēdē emoicheusen autēn en tē kardia autou.
A close translation is:
“He has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Already.
Not someday.
Not only if the opportunity becomes physical.
Already, in the heart.
The Greek word kardia refers here to the inner person—the center of thoughts, desires, intentions, and moral commitments.
Jesus is not merely concerned with whether your hands remained innocent.
He is concerned with what your heart has chosen to entertain.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
When you deliberately open pornography to sexually desire someone on the screen, what exactly are you doing with your heart?
You are not simply observing a picture.
You are intentionally directing sexual desire toward someone.
You may never meet that person.
You may never know their name.
You may never physically touch them.
But distance does not automatically make lust innocent.
A screen cannot turn something Jesus calls sinful into something spiritually harmless.
That is why the honest biblical answer is this:
Deliberately watching pornography for the purpose of lust ordinarily falls under the heart-level sexual sin Jesus condemns in Matthew 5:28.
But we must be careful to say exactly what Scripture says—and no more.

Jesus did not mention modern internet pornography by name. He was addressing lustful looking and the commandment against adultery. Nor does His teaching mean that every form of sexual sin is identical in its circumstances, consequences, or responsibilities.

Physical adultery is a distinct act of sexual unfaithfulness. Lustful looking is a real sin of the heart. Both matter before God, but they should not be carelessly treated as identical in every respect.
For a married person, pornography can also violate the trust and sexual faithfulness promised within marriage, even though it is not the same physical act as an extramarital sexual encounter.
For an unmarried person, deliberately cultivating lust remains morally serious. Jesus' teaching is not permission for single people to indulge desires simply because they have no spouse.

And for anyone who has encountered sexual content accidentally, experienced an unwanted intrusive thought, or felt temptation without choosing to indulge it, this passage should not be twisted into an accusation that temptation alone makes them an adulterer.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
The distinction between temptation and chosen lust matters.
Not because we want to make sin smaller.
But because we must never make Scripture say something it does not say.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
Long before pornography could be streamed through a phone, God had already revealed that sexual faithfulness involved more than avoiding physical acts.
Exodus 20:14 declares:
“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”
And Exodus 20:17 also commands God's people not to covet their neighbor's wife.
In Hebrew, the command against coveting uses the verb:
לֹא תַחְמֹד
Lo tachmod.
“You shall not covet.”
The command addresses wrongful desire, not merely outward action.
Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5 does not invent the idea that God cares about the heart. It brings the moral depth of God's law into unmistakable focus.
God has always cared about what happens where no one else can see.
And that is where pornography becomes more than a private habit.
Because the world tells you that if nobody gets hurt, nothing is wrong.
But pornography is not automatically harmless because it is consumed privately.
It can train you to approach another person's body as something to consume rather than a person to honor.
It can normalize secrecy.
It can feed dissatisfaction.
It can undermine trust when hidden within a relationship.
It can involve material produced through exploitation or coercion, though not every production has the same circumstances.
And it can become a repeated escape from pain without ever addressing the pain itself.

Not everyone who views pornography develops a compulsive pattern. Not every struggling marriage can blame pornography for its difficulties. And it would be irresponsible to pretend that every person experiences exactly the same psychological effects.
But none of those qualifications erase the spiritual question Jesus places before us.
What is this practice cultivating in your heart?
Perhaps you started watching out of curiosity.
Perhaps you encountered it when you were far too young to understand what you were seeing.
Perhaps you were exposed to sexual material before you even knew how to name the shame that followed.
Perhaps it became a refuge when you felt rejected.
Perhaps loneliness made it feel like companionship.
Perhaps stress made it feel like relief.
Perhaps betrayal made it feel like control.
Perhaps you kept returning because, for a few moments, it helped you forget the emptiness you did not know how to explain.
And now the habit feels stronger than the promises you make.
But hear this carefully.
Understanding how a struggle began is not the same as excusing every choice that followed.
And taking responsibility for your choices does not require denying the wounds that may have made you vulnerable.
Both things can be true.
You may need repentance.
You may also need healing.
You may need accountability.
You may also need to grieve what happened to you.
And none of those needs places you beyond the mercy of Jesus Christ.
This is where many believers misunderstand holiness.
They think the Christian life is simply a matter of becoming better at hiding temptation.
So they delete their browsing history.
They change their passwords.
They make another promise.
They avoid eye contact at church.
They sing louder during worship because they hope the sound will drown out the guilt.
And for a few days, they feel victorious.
Until the loneliness returns.
Until the stress returns.
Until the familiar opportunity returns.
Then the cycle begins again.
Sin.
Regret.
Promises.
Silence.
Sin.
Regret.
Promises.
Silence.
But Jesus did not die on the cross merely to help you become more sophisticated at managing appearances.
He came to reconcile sinners to God and transform them by His grace.
And transformation begins when we stop confusing secrecy with safety.
Listen to what Jesus says immediately after His warning about lust.
Matthew 5:29 speaks of tearing out the right eye if it causes a person to sin.
Those words are deliberately shocking.
Jesus is using forceful, figurative language to communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin.
He is not commanding self-mutilation or physical self-harm.
The point is that sin must not be treated casually, even when resisting it requires painful sacrifices.
In our world, that might mean removing an application you keep returning to.
It might mean changing how and where you use your phone.
It might mean refusing to take your devices into situations where secrecy repeatedly becomes an opportunity.
It might mean using content filters and accountability tools.
It might mean confessing to a trustworthy mature Christian rather than pretending you are fighting successfully alone.
It might mean seeking qualified professional support when the behavior has become compulsive or is connected to trauma, anxiety, or other difficulties.
It might mean having an honest conversation with a spouse about broken trust, with appropriate care for their feelings and safety.
And yes, it might mean losing access to something your flesh has learned to crave.
Because genuine repentance is not merely feeling terrible after sin.
It involves turning away from sin and turning toward God.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω (metanoeō), which carries the sense of changing one's mind or turning in repentance.
Biblical repentance is not just a moment of emotional intensity.
It bears fruit in a changed direction.
And that changed direction is possible only because God's grace meets us where we truly are.
Not where we pretend to be.
Think about David.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man who knew the language of prayer.
And yet a man who committed grievous sexual sin and then abused his power in an attempt to conceal it.
David's sin in 2 Samuel 11 was far more than a private lustful thought. It involved adultery, a grave misuse of authority, and the arranged death of Uriah.
We should never flatten the suffering of those harmed by his actions merely to turn his story into a comforting illustration.
But when David was confronted, Psalm 51 records his plea for mercy.
Psalm 51:10 says:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The word bara, translated “create,” is especially striking.
David is not merely asking God to help him polish his reputation.
He is pleading for inward renewal.
He knows that his deepest problem cannot be solved by appearing righteous again.
He needs God's mercy.
He needs a clean heart.
And perhaps that is the prayer you have been avoiding.
Not because you do not believe in God.
But because you know that asking for a clean heart means surrendering the secret place you have tried to keep for yourself.
You cannot sincerely ask Jesus to rule your life while insisting that one cherished sin remains beyond His authority.
But neither should you imagine that His willingness to receive you depends on first achieving flawless self-control.
The Gospel is not that the already-clean are welcomed.
It is that Christ came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we achieved a perfect record.
Not after we could look back at six months of uninterrupted victory.
Christ died for sinners.
That includes the believer who has stumbled again.
That includes the person whose hidden life contradicts their public testimony.
That includes the husband who has betrayed his wife's trust.
That includes the wife who has cultivated secret fantasies and feels ashamed to admit it.
That includes the young adult who has never known what life looks like without access to pornography.
And that includes the person reading this who is not even sure whether they can still call themselves a Christian.
But the cross is not permission to make peace with sin.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of mercy meet.
The same Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
And following Him means learning to surrender the desires that compete with His lordship.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood in public humiliation while her accusers sought to use her situation against Him.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those accusers, and the account concludes with His words:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11
There is a textual detail worth acknowledging: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and modern Bible editions commonly mark the passage accordingly.
It should therefore be handled with appropriate care rather than treated as an uncontested foundation for doctrine.
Nevertheless, the mercy and call to holiness expressed in the account are consistent with teachings clearly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus does not celebrate sin.
And He does not present mercy as indifference to it.
He calls people out of darkness and into new life.
That is the beautiful tension at the center of the Gospel.
Grace does not say your sin was harmless.
Grace says your sin does not have to be your final story.
Forgiveness does not mean that broken trust instantly disappears.
It does not mean that wounded spouses must pretend they are no longer wounded.
It does not erase the need for honesty, responsibility, wise boundaries, or patient rebuilding.
But it means that failure does not have to become your permanent identity.
And perhaps this is the part someone desperately needs to hear.
You are not required to call your chains freedom just because you have grown accustomed to wearing them.
You may have spent years believing that pornography is simply part of being human.
That everyone does it.
That nobody can really change.
That resisting is unrealistic.
That marriage will automatically cure it.
That finding the right partner will remove every temptation.
But marriage is not a cure for an unaddressed pattern of lust.
A spouse is not responsible for becoming the solution to another person's sinful choices.
And sexual intimacy within marriage was never designed to replace spiritual maturity.
First Thessalonians 4:3–5 says:

“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God.”

Christians differ on some details of how verse 4 should be translated, particularly the expression concerning one's “vessel.” But the passage's central concern is unmistakable: God's people are called to sexual holiness, honor, and self-control rather than lustful passion.
Notice the word honour.
Honor changes the way we look at people.
Honor remembers that the person on the screen is a human being.
Someone with dignity.
Someone whose life cannot be reduced to a body.
Someone made in the image of God.
Someone who is not there merely to satisfy your imagination.
And this is one of pornography's deepest spiritual dangers.
It can teach the heart to separate desire from love, intimacy from covenant, and bodies from personhood.
The Gospel calls us in the opposite direction.
Toward love that honors.
Toward desire governed by holiness.
Toward relationships shaped by truth.
Toward a vision of other people that reflects the dignity God has given them.
Now imagine something.
Imagine your child growing up in a world where explicit material is available within seconds.
Imagine them learning about intimacy from people who do not know them, love them, or care about their spiritual formation.
Imagine them believing that bodies exist to be consumed and that affection is something to demand rather than something to give.
Would you want that for them?
Would you want them to inherit the same secrecy that has exhausted you?
The point is not to burden parents with the false belief that their personal struggles automatically determine their children's future.
It is to recognize that our choices, conversations, examples, and willingness to seek help can shape the spiritual atmosphere of our homes.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony you can give your family is not the claim that you have never struggled.
It is the evidence that when you recognized sin, you humbled yourself, sought help, and began walking in truth.
Children need to know that God's holiness is real.
They also need to know that His mercy is real.
And adults need that same reminder.
Because there is another danger in the fight against pornography.
It is possible to become so consumed with your own failure that you begin to treat shame as though it were the voice of God.
But conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction brings sin into the light and calls us toward repentance.
Destructive shame tells us that hiding is our only option.
Conviction says, “This must change.”
Shame says, “You can never change.”
Conviction calls us toward Christ.
Shame tempts us to run away from Him.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The assurance of this verse belongs to those who are in Christ. It is not a declaration that sin no longer matters.
It is a declaration that those united to Jesus are no longer under the condemnation from which He has rescued them.
And Romans 8 continues by describing life through the Spirit.
That is why freedom is more than the absence of pornography.
Freedom is learning to live under the gracious rule of Christ.
Freedom is being able to tell the truth.
Freedom is treating people with dignity.
Freedom is cultivating self-control.
Freedom is pursuing reconciliation where trust has been broken.
Freedom is learning how to face loneliness, anxiety, disappointment, and pain without repeatedly running to a secret escape.
Freedom is no longer organizing your life around protecting what you know is harming your obedience to God.
And this kind of growth may involve a long process.
Some people experience decisive changes quickly.
Others face repeated temptation while developing healthier patterns and deeper accountability.
Progress is not always linear.
A setback should not be excused, but neither must it be interpreted as proof that Christ has abandoned you.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Confession is not a magical formula that allows us to indulge sin without repentance.
It is part of walking honestly before the God whose forgiveness is grounded in Jesus Christ.
And the invitation remains open.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn toward the Savior.
Do not wait until you feel worthy enough to pray.
Do not wait until your life looks impressive enough to seek Christian fellowship.
Do not wait until you have achieved some imaginary standard of perfection before you begin taking practical steps toward holiness.
Start where you are.
If you have fallen today, confess it today.
If you need help, ask for help.
If you have deceived someone, take responsibility with wisdom and care.
If the habit has become compulsive, seek appropriate support.
If you have experienced exploitation or abuse, remember that what was done to you was not your sin, and seeking protection and healing is not a failure of faith.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you thought God was finished with you, remember Peter.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
The man who promised loyalty failed in the hour of testing.
Yet in John 21, the risen Christ met Peter and restored him to a calling of love and service.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's mercy was real.
Your story is not Peter's story in every detail.
But Peter's restoration reveals something precious about the Savior.
Jesus is not powerless in the presence of human failure.
He knows how to restore the repentant.
He knows how to call the fallen back to faithfulness.
And He knows how to build a future that does not require pretending the past never happened.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they have never sinned.
Not to make wounded believers feel permanently disqualified.
Not to turn conviction into public humiliation.
But to proclaim the biblical truth that Jesus Christ saves sinners, calls them to repentance, and forms them into disciples who increasingly reflect His character.
And if this article has reached a part of your life you rarely speak about, please do not let the moment pass as another emotional experience that changes nothing.
You do not need to disclose explicit details, reveal private information, or confess intimate experiences publicly. A simple request for prayer is enough.
If God has already helped you grow through this battle, consider sharing a testimony that gives Him glory without exposing anyone else's private life.
Someone reading the comments may need to know that repentance is possible and that they are not the only person seeking help.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
But because a message of biblical truth and hope may reach someone who would never have the courage to ask for it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, Christians who have grown complacent, and even those who are still exploring faith.
They may not agree with every word immediately.
But they deserve the opportunity to hear what Jesus actually taught.
And there is something else I want to place before you—not as pressure, but as an invitation to participate in a work you believe is worth sustaining.
Every article shared, every biblical resource made accessible, and every opportunity to encourage a struggling believer requires time, effort, and ongoing support.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Christ.
These resources are intended to nourish faith, strengthen biblical understanding, encourage repentance, and equip believers to follow Jesus beyond a single emotional moment.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Not because anyone can purchase spiritual blessing.
But freely, thoughtfully, and joyfully, if you believe in the mission and have the means to support it.
These products can serve as reminders of faith and opportunities to share encouragement, but they are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
Jesus is.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share truth with love matters.
Because this ministry is not ultimately about growing an audience.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
Now, before you leave, return with me to that quiet room.
The screen has gone dark.
The guilt has returned.
The familiar thoughts begin to whisper that nothing will ever change.
But imagine that this time, instead of hiding, you open your Bible.
Instead of making another empty promise, you confess honestly.
Instead of protecting the habit, you begin removing what keeps feeding it.
Instead of isolating yourself, you reach out for help.
Instead of defining yourself by your latest failure, you remember the cross.
You remember that Jesus knows the truth about you.
All of it.
The history.
The secrecy.
The excuses.
The fear.
The choices you regret.
The wounds you have not yet learned how to describe.
And still, His Gospel calls you to come.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
But because His grace is sufficient to forgive and His Spirit is powerful to transform.
The Savior who taught that lust matters in the heart is the same Savior who gave His life for sinners.
The One who said that purity is deeper than outward behavior is the One who can renew the inward person.
The One who refuses to call darkness light is the One who invites us to walk in His light.
That is the answer to the question.

Yes, deliberately looking at pornography to indulge lust falls under the heart-level sexual sin Jesus condemned. His teaching in Matthew 5:28 makes clear that sexual faithfulness is not merely a matter of physical restraint.
But the Gospel does not end with the exposure of sin.
It leads us to the cross.
To repentance.
To forgiveness.
To restoration.
To a new way of living through the grace of God.
And if you have been waiting for the day when you finally feel strong enough to come back to Jesus, do not build your hope on that feeling.
Come to Him in your weakness.
Tell Him the truth.
Ask Him for a clean heart.
Take the next faithful step.
And keep following Him.
Because the deepest miracle is not merely that you stop looking at what once enslaved you.
It is that you begin to see Christ as more precious than the sin you once refused to surrender.
If it gave you hope, save it and return to the Scriptures when the battle feels heavy.
Remember this, especially when the night is quiet and the temptation feels stronger than your resolve:
The screen may remember what you searched for, but the cross declares that your past does not have to write the ending of your story.
